To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ribosome infidelity does not appear to be a major factor in the appearance of altered proteins in aging animals.

(i) the rate of protein synthesis by isolated rabbit liver ribosomes declines with age; (ii) this decline is associated with a decrease in the rate of peptide bond formation; (iii) the decline in the rate of synthesis of individual polypeptides is greater than the decline in the total synthesis; and (iv) the decline in peptide bond formation cannot be accounted for by a decrease in ribosome number or by a decrease in the number of ribosomal subunits per cell.

(a) the fidelity characteristics of ribosomes from young and old animals are not significantly different; (b) the ribosomal infidelity model of age-related protein alterations does not appear to be a viable mechanism; and (c) the ribosomal error-catastrophe model of aging, as proposed by Orgel, does not seem to be a viable model for explaining the aging phenomenon.
